1. What we did

We found a bug in the Biome Markdown formatter and fixed it.

Bug: A list item can end with a blockquote. In that case, the formatter removed the blank line after the blockquote.
Result of the bug: The next paragraph became part of the blockquote. On the second run, the formatter added > before that paragraph. So the formatter changed the meaning of the document, and the output was different on each run.
Cause: The function list_ends_with_line_break checks the last block of the last list item. It only recognised leaf elements and list items. A blockquote is neither of these, so the function returned false. Four other parts of the formatter used this incorrect value. Each of those parts is correct by itself, so the error became visible only at the last step.

markdown/auxiliary/newline.rs: We did not change this file. It now gets the correct value, so it keeps the Newline node.

Result: The output keeps the blank line, and the paragraph stays outside the blockquote. The second output is the same as the first output.

Changes from your plan:
Our initial plan was to wrap grouped connectors inside Graphviz `subgraph cluster_*` blocks
    and rely entirely on Graphviz's default layout algorithm to route wires cleanly. 
  
    Where we hit a bottleneck (The Wire Clustering / Spiderweb Bug):
    When testing our grouping implementation against realistic, high-pin-density circuits 
    (16-pin LCD subassembly in demo-sharan and ESP32 with sensors in demo-7), we hit severe
    layout degradation: 
    1. Enclosing nodes inside cluster boxes restricts Graphviz's vertical ranking degrees of
    freedom.
    2. Inverted wire-to-pin sequences created bezier spline crossings, turning inter-module     
    wiring into a tangled spiderweb.
    3. Full 16-pin connector tables ballooned vertically when unpopulated pins remained visible,
    forcing steep wire angles and pin pinch points. 
  
    How we adapted:                                                                             
    Rather than abandoning native Graphviz clusters, we diagnosed the layout engine mechanics   
    and established four ergonomic wiring patterns:                                             
    - Monotonic Pin Ordering: Strictly ordering conductor indexes to match connector pin rows,  
    producing straight parallel splines with zero crossings.                                    
    - Local Subassembly Loops (`loops:`): Routing common rails (GND, 5V) internally on the      
    connector table rather than traversing long external cables.                                
    - Pin Trimming (`hide_disconnected_pins: true`): Collapsing inactive pins to reduce         
    connector table height.                                                                     
    - Port Face Segregation: Splitting ingress power/data on the left face and downstream       
    routing on the right face.

What you built:
Fix for JupyterLab issue #20372: after a page reload, Restart Kernel restarts the wrong kernel.

Root cause: for a notebook opened with "Notebook (no kernel)" (shouldReuse: false), the context has no session. When a kernel was selected, changeKernel() therefore called startNew() and renamed the new session onto the notebook's path, although the server already had a session for that path. Two sessions shared one path; after a reload the notebook attached to the older one, so Restart Kernel hit a different kernel than the one running the code.

What works:
- packages/apputils/src/sessioncontext.tsx: changeKernel() now calls a new private method, _connectToPathSession(), before _changeKernel(). If the context has no session, it refreshes the running sessions, finds the one whose path matches the notebook, and connects to it. The existing kernel-change code then changes that session's kernel, so no second session is created. If no session exists, the old creation path runs unchanged. If the refresh fails, it logs a warning and falls back to the old behaviour. About 30 added lines.
- shouldReuse and the "Notebook (no kernel)" behaviour are untouched.
- packages/apputils/test/sessioncontext.spec.ts: 9 new Jest tests (existing session reused; selecting the session's own kernel keeps it; stale session list; concurrent requests; no session on the path; different path not reused; reload reattaches to the new kernel; connection error; refresh failure). 5 of them fail without the fix and pass with it.

In progress / not done:
- No browser (Galata) test and no recorded demo yet.
- Known limitation: two overlapping kernel requests could race on a session that was just renamed. Not mitigated.
- Existing duplicate sessions are not repaired. A session that vanishes between lookup and kernel change shows the normal error dialog.
- Open question for maintainers: choosing a kernel spec replaces the existing session's kernel (same as Change Kernel in other notebooks). Keeping it when the name matches is not implemented.

Changes from your plan:
1. Where the Change Lives
- Initially, I planned to implement the session lookup inside _changeKernel(), which would have required approximately 20 additional lines of code and an _isTerminating guard.
- However, I moved the lookup into the public changeKernel() method and introduced a private helper function.
- The reason was that _changeKernel() is also called during the automatic kernel startup when a notebook is opened. Implementing the lookup there would have introduced an unnecessary additional server request every time a notebook was opened.
- I also discovered that the _isTerminating guard was unnecessary because a terminating context still has an associated session. Therefore, I removed it.
2. Understanding Kernel Behaviour
- Initially, I assumed that attaching to an existing session would automatically preserve its running kernel.
- However, after examining the jupyter_server implementation and reproducing its REST API calls, I discovered that changing a session's kernel using a kernel specification name actually:
  - Starts a new kernel.
  - Shuts down the previously running kernel.
- Therefore, the fix replaces the kernel when a different kernel is selected, consistent with the existing Change Kernel behaviour.
- If the user selects the same kernel that the session is already using, the existing kernel is preserved.
- I added separate tests to verify both behaviours.

Changes from your plan:
1. Fast-Path Jordan Validation: In Round 2, our conceptual proposal considered `len(blocks) == mat.cols` to decide diagonalizability. Code inspection revealed `blocks` in SymPy stores eigenvalue instances, not block objects. We adapted our implementation to collect independent nullspace basis vectors first (`len(jordan_basis) == mat.cols`) and added a strict rank verification guard (`basis_mat.rank() == mat.cols`) before returning, falling back cleanly to full generalized eigenvector chain computation if the matrix is defective.

2. Minimal Symbolic Disturbance: Rather than forcibly rewriting all symbolic eigenvalues into a canonical representation (which could alter user-expected expressions or cause performance regressions), we implemented a zero-difference equivalence check `_iszero(_simplify(eigenvalue - existing)) is True`. This preserves the original expression representations while accurately accumulating multiplicities.

3. Cloud Container & Shallow Clone Resilience: Streamlit Cloud and CI runners perform shallow Git checkouts (`--depth=1`) without release tags, causing SymPy's default `release.py` to raise an `ImportError`. We created `sympy/_version.py` and added a graceful development version fallback in `sympy/release.py` to guarantee zero-crash execution across any cloud environment.

What you built: We have implemented a production-level fix for Biome issue #10784 in crates/biome_js_analyze/src/lint/style/use_unified_type_signatures.rs. At the beginning of Rule::action(), the analyzer checks state.parameters_to_merge and immediately returns None if any parameter requires the MergeParameterOperation::MakeOptional operation, preventing an unsafe code action before any syntax mutation is created. The diagnostic functionality remains unchanged, so developers still receive the warning, “This overload signature can be combined with a similar one,” while unsafe automatic fixes are suppressed. At the same time, safe automated fixes are preserved: overloads with union-compatible parameter types can still be merged, identical duplicate signatures can still be removed, and overloads containing parameters that were already optional can still receive safe cleanup fixes. We have also added a dedicated regression test fixture at crates/biome_js_analyze/tests/specs/style/useUnifiedTypeSignatures/issue_10784.ts, along with its snapshot and updates to invalid.ts.snap, covering the affected upstream cases. For release preparation, we added an official Biome changeset at .changeset/fix-10784-use-unified-type-signatures.md with patch release metadata. We deliberately avoided implementing full semantic type synthesis across separate modules because Biome is primarily a syntactic linter rather than a complete TypeScript type checker; suppressing only the unsafe code action while retaining the diagnostic is a focused solution that fits Biome's architecture.
Changes from your plan: During Round 2, we initially considered suppressing fixes whenever two overloads had different parameter counts, but testing revealed that this approach would also block safe fixes. For example, in update(id: number) and update(id: number, name?: string), the second parameter is already optional, so the merge does not introduce a new optional parameter and the cleanup remains safe. We therefore changed the approach to check specifically for MergeParameterOperation::MakeOptional, which prevents only the unsafe mutation while preserving safe fixes.
